1:
Calvin explains why the search is proposed at all. Scripture testifies that God waits for repentance, so it may seem strange that he rises so severely against his own Church; but the ungodly accuse him of cruelty, and he shows here that he was not at liberty to forgive. Even if I would, he has God say, I could not. Calvin grants this is spoken after the manner of men, and takes it to mean that every expedient was tried before extreme severity. Keil and Delitzsch states the same ground in a line, that by reason of universal godlessness the Lord cannot pardon, and renders the clause as seeking faithfulness rather than truth. Calvin also distinguishes the places named: the streets are the narrow lanes where the poor lived, the broad places the squares of the chief men, so the search covers both.

Henry reads it as a challenge to produce a single honest man. Jerusalem had become like the old world in which all flesh corrupted its way; some flattered themselves that many good men were left to stand in the gap, others boasted that this was the holy city, but God bids them search the town. Look in the streets where they converse and the broad places where they keep their markets, Henry says, and see whether you can find a magistrate who does justice impartially. And if there is here and there a conscientious man, you will not find him in public, for he dares not appear lest he be abused and run down; truth has fallen in the street and is forced to seek out corners. Gill takes the command as addressed not to the prophet only but to anyone who cared to look into the reasons of God's dealings. Wesley makes the searchers all the earth, so that God vindicates himself before the whole world; and he sets the offer against an older one, since God condescends to pardon this city for one righteous man where he once came no lower than ten. Ellicott presses the comparison to its end: there were not ten righteous found in Sodom, and in Jerusalem not one.

Ellicott raises a difficulty of date. The dark shades hardly suit a reign described elsewhere as one of thorough reformation, and he allows two answers: that parts may have been worked up when the prophecies were rewritten under a later king, or that the prophet saw at the time how hollow that reformation was.

The oath raises an obvious objection, which Gill states: multitudes made mention of the name of the Lord and swore by it, so a man of integrity should not have been hard to find. Clarke answers that though they professed to bind themselves by that name, they swore falsely, since not believing in him they took an oath by which they did not think themselves bound. Wesley says it shortly, that they used the form of an oath but neither in truth nor righteousness. Ellicott finds something more particular, that a distinction between the binding force of different formulas of adjuration, like the one the later scribes drew, was already in some degree current, and that the guilt of these men was to use the most solemn formula of all and be perjured in it. Traces of swearing by other gods appear later in the chapter, with which this oath seems contrasted. Calvin makes this an anticipation of an excuse. The Jews supposed that having God's name continually in their mouths covered all their vices; but the prophet shows the disguise was worthless, since in so using the name they profaned it. He goes further: it is one thing to lack the fear of God in common practice, and worse when the only religious thing about a people is itself sacrilege, for to dishonour God to his face is a monstrous impiety.
3:
Calvin begins with a warning about the chapter divisions. Some pervert this verse, as though the prophet meant that God would not turn his eyes from what was right because he meant to execute vengeance; but the subject is unbroken, and those who divided the verses have often unknowingly perverted the meaning. The numbers are worth keeping as a help to memory, Calvin says, but the divisions hinder readers, for it is preposterous to blend what is separate and divide what is connected. Read continuously, the sense is that the Jews avowed God's name in vain and made a show of religion by ceremonies, since God searches the heart and cares nothing for external masks. Calvin also notices to whom the words are spoken. The prophet turns to God, which shows he was wearied with addressing the people and prevailed nothing with the obstinate; he might have gone on reasoning with them, but he breaks off and leaves them, as one who finds he is addressing rocks and stones.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word for truth carries no article and implies faithfulness, truth in the inward parts as well as in words, and that God looked for this and found a temper that hardens itself against discipline and refuses to repent. Gill draws out the same: God has no regard to hypocritical worshippers but to the upright, looking not at appearances but at the heart; his respect is to those who have a true sense of sin and make a hearty confession, and he is nigh to the man of a contrite spirit, while he has no regard to the disfigured faces of formalists or the tears of a profane man. Wesley glosses the verbs that follow: not grieving means they have not repented, and being consumed means God did not chastise lightly but wasted them by several enemies, and yet they profited nothing.

The plea of ignorance is read two ways. Gill takes the prophet to have reasoned that reproofs had no effect because these people were poor, so busy earning bread that they were neither at leisure to attend to divine things nor of capacity to receive correction. Clarke states it in a line: they are ignorant, have no education, and know no better. Ellicott corrects the opening word, literally and rather than therefore, and calls this a half-pitying plea for the poor: looking on the masses that toil for bread, whom the scribes afterwards called the people of the earth, it is not strange that men left untaught should have learnt so little, a thought paralleled in the compassion shown to sheep without a shepherd. He defines the way of the Lord as what God approves.

Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin treat the plea as a device. Keil and Delitzsch says the want of good faith is found not only in the lower orders but in the higher ranks of the educated, and that the point is put in this shape so that the prophet, supposing at first that only the common people are so sunk, may turn to the great and discover among them a thorough-going renunciation of the law; the weak, he adds, live from hand to mouth with their anxieties bent on food and clothing, and do foolishly for want of religious training. Calvin is sharper: some think the prophet is excusing the people and extenuating their fault, and they are greatly mistaken, for by this comparison he shows how far past remedy things were, corruption prevailing not among the multitude only but among the chief men, so that no soundness was left from head to sole. He might have said plainly that the chief men were corrupt as well as the lowest, but the comparison is more striking, since it lets the reader suppose for a moment that the ignorant may be excused and greater integrity found higher up.
5:
Who the great men are is agreed. Gill names the princes and nobles and judges, the elders of the people and the doctors of the law; Calvin adds the priests and prophets, the king's counsellors and the king himself. Ellicott hears a grave and indignant irony in the turn, the prophet repeating for the great the very words that describe the wisdom he failed to find among the poor and now hopes to find higher up. Calvin insists the inquiry was not made in doubt: the purpose was to shame the chief men and confirm what had been said, that not one just man could be found in the city; the prophet speaks as the thing appeared probable, since common opinion held that rulers were well acquainted with the law. Ellicott would render the clause that follows less ambiguously as surely they too, noting that it begins with the same word as the preceding verse, and takes the sense to be that great and poor alike are altogether evil, the educated even more defiant than the ignorant. Clarke says these had cast aside all restraint and trampled moral obligation under their feet, sweeping the lower classes along with them, and quotes an ancient lawgiver's saying that laws are cobwebs which entangle the small flies while the great go through and carry all away. Wesley says only that these are more refractory than the others, and that no law of God can hold them.

The three beasts of the next verse divide the voices sharply. Gill, Clarke and Wesley take them for the invading king and his army, Gill reading the forest as the populous city he came from, Wesley distributing the figures so that the lion denotes power and pride, the wolf greediness, and the leopard not speed only but vigilance and subtlety. Clarke assigns the same three qualities and reports another scholar's view that a different northern people is meant. Ellicott keeps the figure but leaves the reference open: the three forms of ferocity perhaps represent fierceness, ravenousness and cunning, or possibly three oppressors in whom those attributes were impersonated. All three animals were common in that country, he grants, but he thinks it a weak rendering of the prophet's words to take them literally as a prediction that the land would be ravaged by beasts of prey, and he notes that the same three appear together in the opening canto of a famous poem.

Keil and Delitzsch stands against all of them. The verse, he says, is neither a threatening of future punishments nor to be taken figuratively, the beasts standing for enemies; the change of tense tells against the future construction and shows the verbs are used of chastisements already partly suffered. Calvin knows the same dispute in a milder form. Some render the words in the past tense, so that the prophet reminds the Jews they had not been afflicted without reason and had deserved heavier punishments; but Calvin notes that the tenses often change in Hebrew and is inclined to the future, since the prophet seems not to be recording what they had suffered but reminding them of what awaited them. He also weighs the second animal. Some render it the wolf of the evening, which he allows, since hungry wolves are elsewhere so called, running furiously at nightfall after a day's fruitless hunting; but because the lion comes from the forest he thinks it likelier the wolf comes from the desert, and observes that the word here is never used for the evening. Ellicott prefers the deserts too, though he grants that the evening sense is supported by two other prophets.
7:
The opening question is not a real one. Gill reports three constructions of the particle, that it is a word of exclamation, or of admiration, or the equivalent of a negative, so that the sentence becomes a fixed resolution not to pardon, followed by the reasons. Calvin calls the form what rhetoricians name a conference, in which God seeks the judgment of the adverse party on a cause already clear, which is itself a proof of confidence, as advocates deliberate with an opponent when they wish to show that nothing is doubtful. The sense is that God was constrained by necessity: if I am the judge of the world, can men who provoke me so openly escape? I should expose my own glory to ridicule and in a manner deny myself if I did not punish a people so irreclaimable.

The clause about feeding is disputed at the level of the text. Ellicott says the Hebrew text itself gives, though I had bound them by oath, that is by the covenant, as of marriage, which heightens the enormity of what follows and yields a better sense than the received rendering, taken from the margin; and he thinks there is probably an implied reference to the covenant sworn in the reign of Josiah. Wesley keeps the received sense and draws the moral in a line, that such is the natural effect of unsanctified prosperity. On the houses, Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the singular, perhaps because the prophet thinks primarily of the idol's temple as the scene of the guilt, which here as elsewhere symbolises national apostasy. Clarke says the places meant are those consecrated to idolatry, since in the language of the prophets adultery generally signifies idolatry; though at the next verse he allows the charge may also have been literally true, since the abominations of that worship would produce such a state of things.

The comparison with horses is obscure in one word. Gill explains why the animal is chosen and reports a Greek rendering that makes them horses maddened after the females; on the word translated in the morning he gives an alternative meaning drawing out, and admits the term is difficult. Ellicott renders the line as fed stallion horses they rove about, and takes the animal passion to answer both to the same passion in men and to the lust for an idolatrous ritual. Calvin weighs two derivations, one giving armed and the other fed, and asks what sense armed horses could have; he keeps fed, and dismisses as far-fetched the notion that the men rose early after their adultery to exhibit their disgrace. The comparison is meant, he says, to show that no chastity or honesty was left: to say every man lay in wait for his neighbour's bed would have been heinous by itself, but the prophet makes them worse, differing in nothing from lustful horses well fed and strong.

Calvin treats the closing question as the same figure returning. God holds a conference with them again, to check their complaints and close their mouths before they object that they were too severely treated; the answer is that it was impossible not to punish wicked men who would not repent. Since God is the Judge of the world he can no more surrender his judgment than his essence, and his majesty and his office are inseparably joined, so that what the Jews thought possible was not. Calvin marks the difference from human courts: an earthly judge may pardon the worst of men, but God pardons only by leading sinners to repentance and so never suffers sin to go unpunished; the man who repents becomes his own judge and anticipates God's. Gill states the plain sense beside it, that the visiting is for such adulteries and lasciviousness, and in the way of punishment.
10:
Calvin explains the device of the command. God addresses through his prophet the enemies whom he had appointed to be ministers of his vengeance, and the prophets often speak so when they wish to rouse men more sharply, knowing how great their indifference is when God summons them to judgment. Simple instruction availed little, and the representation is far more penetrating when the prophet, at God's command, musters the enemy like a celestial herald and tells them what to do. Calvin adds what the first clause takes away: the Jews boasted in vain of the height of their walls, since God would make their enemies climb them, so that entrance would not be difficult. Gill reads it the same way, as an order to the invaders to ascend and break down the walls, as they did, and draws the general rule that nothing is done without the Lord's will and that there is no evil in a city but what he does or orders or suffers. Wesley puts it as a direct commission, to go and execute vengeance and lay the city and all its fortifications level with the ground, and takes the last clause as a disowning. Henry says the same in a word, that God disowns them and dooms them to destruction, and then asks whether there is not a cause.

What is to be taken away is the crux of the verse. Ellicott would render the first word not walls but her palm-trees, since the Hebrew term is used elsewhere for a mast and here seems to mean the tall stately trunk; and for battlements he would read branches, which carries on the same imagery and marks the limits of a destruction that is not to be a full end. The rendering walls, still kept by some, he allows may refer to the walls of a vineyard, in which case the second word would be the tendrils of the vine; and he notes that both palm and vine appear on later coins as symbols of that nation. Keil and Delitzsch renders the clause as tearing away her tendrils. Clarke reports the same alternatives, branches or vines, and gives the sense as destroying the branches and cutting down the stem while leaving the root undamaged, so that enough of the people should remain for the state to be regenerated; he adds that the old versions read instead, leave her foundations, for they are the Lord's, which agrees well with the command not to make a full end.

The reason follows, and it is a charge of treachery. Calvin explains the verb, which means to deceive or act perfidiously, and insists that God is not complaining of a partial fault but charging general defection, so that both kingdoms alike had become apostates; the construction with its preposition means to deal treacherously with someone, and might be rendered to dissemble. He notices whom the charge covers. The people were by then divided into two kingdoms, and though the prophet had been given especially to the southern tribe it was still his duty to labour for the north, whose kingdom was already in some measure fallen with four tribes driven into exile; he wished to do what good he could to the remnant. Gill divides the two houses the same way and calls the perfidy of both very great and attended with aggravating circumstances. Henry sharpens the point by the irony in it, that two houses at variance with one another agreed in this, to deal very treacherously against God, forsaking his worship and so violating their covenant with him, revolting from him and playing the hypocrite with him.
12:
Whether the charge is lying or denial turns on a preposition. Calvin will not wholly reject the rendering that they lied to God, but argues that it cannot stand: had lying been meant the verb would have taken a different preposition, and with the one used it means simply that they denied him. He supports this from the other places where the verb occurs in the same construction, and observes that the old versions themselves divide. The context, he says, requires denial, since what follows is a flat contradiction of the threatening. Gill reaches the same place another way: they may not have said in express words that there was no God, but in denying his providence and disbelieving his word by the prophets they tacitly denied that he was God, and the sense of the phrase is that he takes no notice of what we do and has given no such orders as these to our enemies. Clarke states it flatly, that they disavowed the Lord and were atheists at heart, and notes that on their own premises the conclusion was just, since if there is no judge there will be no judgment. Wesley keeps the milder sense, that they did not believe these words of the prophet to be the word of God.

Ellicott divides the possibilities more carefully. The clause may mean that it is not the Lord who speaks, so that they heard the warnings as the prophet's own and carrying no certainty of sword or famine; or it may deny that God was at work in the sufferings that fell on the people; or it may go further, to the entire denial made by the fool in the psalm.

Calvin uses the next verse to say something about preaching. Nothing can be imagined more abominable than to deny God, yet if his word is not allowed authority it is the same as though men attempted to thrust him out of heaven; so the majesty of God is indissolubly connected with the public preaching of his truth. He allows that the Jews may not have vented such language openly, but their contempt for the prophets was so gross that the impiety was conspicuous in their whole manner of life.

The mockers' words are read as a taunt with a sting in the tail. Gill takes the first clause to mean that the prophecies shall vanish into air and never be accomplished. Clarke gives the speech in the mockers' own voice: what are the prophets but empty persons, whose words are wind, so that we hear the sound of a threatening and shall hear no more of the matter of it. Wesley calls it a proverbial expression, that all the prophet's threats shall come to nothing and that his words are not from God. On the last clause the voices agree that the speech is still the mockers' and not the prophet's. Ellicott renders it better as a wish, may it so happen to them, the evils the prophets foretell being called down on the prophets' own heads, and notes that the words come from the lips of the unbelieving. Clarke reads it the same way, may their own predictions fall on themselves, and calls this the natural sense of the passage; Wesley says it shall fall on the heads of those who have thus threatened us. Ellicott adds a note on the middle clause, that what is rendered the word is literally he who speaketh, meaning the Lord himself as the speaker, so that the denial is not that a message exists but that anyone is behind it.
14:
The mockers had said the prophets were wind; the answer takes their figure and turns it. Gill states the ground plainly, that because they said it is not the Lord, it is no prophecy of him and therefore shall become wind and come to nothing. Clarke puts the exchange as a retort: they have said they are but air, but I will make them fire, and a fire too that shall devour them, Ellicott notes that the sentence is delivered under the solemn name Jehovah Elohim Zebaoth, used here for the second time in the prophet's teaching, and that the message is divided, partly to the people, because ye speak this word, and partly to the prophet sent to bear witness against them, I will make my words in thy mouth. Wesley reads the consuming agent as the Chaldean army, which shall eat them up like fire.

Calvin makes the verse turn on contempt of the prophets. The will of God from the beginning has been that his servants should be obeyed as though he himself had come down from heaven, so the Jews in despising his prophets dealt no less contumeliously with God than if they had dared to treat him with contempt; and though Christ did not refer to this passage when he said that he who hears you hears me, the saying contains an eternal law. On the figure itself Calvin draws a distinction: elsewhere the word is called fire because it kindles the hearts of men and burns the filth within, a cleansing and not a consuming fire, but here the comparison has a particular meaning, that the prophetic word would consume the people as fire consumes dry wood or straw. Had it been said only that the words would be fire and the people stubble it would not have been expressive enough; the prophet's tongue alone would be more than sufficient. The warning turns back on the reader, that the word appointed for our food may be turned into a fire to us if we obstinately reject it.

Who the far nation is, is answered three ways. Gill says from Babylon. Clarke reports one interpreter for the Scythians and prefers the Babylonians, whose antiquity was great, that empire being founded by Nimrod. Calvin says the Jews thought no danger near them from nations so remote, and the prophet tells them this one was near at hand though coming from far. A second question is who is addressed. Ellicott takes the house of Israel in its wider sense, as including the whole body of the twelve tribes, since there is no contrast with Judah; Wesley takes it for Judah, Israel being already in captivity, called the house of Israel not only because they descended from Jacob but because they were the chief of that stock.

The three descriptions are then weighed. Ellicott gives the strict force of the adjective rendered mighty as lasting or enduring, as used of mountains and of rivers. Calvin takes it not of bravery through age but of hardness and ferocity, adding that antiquity itself inflates the minds of men with pride, since a nation that has ruled from a period out of memory generates spirits more ferocious. On the alien speech Clarke identifies the language as the Chaldee, which though a dialect of the Hebrew is so very different in words and construction that hearing it spoken they could not possibly collect the meaning of what was said. Ellicott observes that to the Jew, as to the Greek, subjection to a people of alien speech added a new element of bitterness. Calvin draws the worst consequence from it: language is the expression of the mind and therefore the bond of society, and where no communication can be made there is no pity to spare the conquered, and none heard who were miserable and might otherwise have obtained some favour.
16:
What makes the quiver like an open grave is disputed. Clarke takes it of marksmanship: they are such exact archers as never to miss, every arrow sure to slay one man. Ellicott reads it much the same way, every arrow a messenger of death, a blast or pestilence from the grave. Gill combines execution and number: their arrows would be very mortal, so that a quiver of them would be as devouring as an open grave into which many dead are cast. He adds that two of the old versions want the clause altogether and that another renders it of throats rather than quivers. Calvin refuses the reading of skill and insists the idea intended is capaciousness. The grave is never satisfied, ready to receive any number, and the quiver would be so large as to hold a vast quantity of arrows, as though it were an open grave. He allows the comparison may seem unnatural at first sight, and explains the eastern manner of fighting behind it, that they had no pitched battles but pretended a flight and then turning hurled their darts. That they are all mighty men he takes as notice that this would be no slight conflict but a certain ruin.

The list of what is devoured is read as a single sweep. Gill takes the harvest of the standing corn, cut down and given as fodder to their horses as armies usually do, or else the increase gathered into the barn and consumed by so great a host. Ellicott makes a grammatical observation that changes the sense: there is no relative pronoun in the Hebrew, so the clause stands parallel with the others and reads that they shall eat, that is destroy, thy sons and thy daughters, as all the older versions translate it; in the other clauses the verb is singular, the invading army being the subject. Calvin notices the same change of number and renders the second verb passively, devoured shall be thy sons and thy daughters, remarking how closely the language resembles that of Moses in the law. His comment is on the cruelty of the use made of victory rather than on the troubles of war: he takes it as granted the enemy would be conqueror and shews only that they would spare neither boys nor girls, since it is hard to be deprived of food but more dreadful for parents to see their children slain. On the last clause Ellicott prefers break down or shatter to impoverish, and takes the sword for battle-axes and other weapons used against cities; Calvin applies the word to every part of the verse, so that by right of the sword the conquerors lay waste the whole country.

Whether the closing verse relieves the sentence or deepens it divides the readers sharply. Ellicott takes it as tempering, the extremest sentence assured not to be absolutely final, intended to be reformatory and not merely penal. Calvin reports that nearly all interpreters think a hope is here given to the faithful, and that he knows no one who takes another view; yet considering the context he feels constrained to take it as enhancing the severity of the vengeance. The particle rendered also is emphatic: when the enemy has stripped the land of its produce and its inhabitants, not even then will the pursuit cease, for scourges will remain when they think rest is given and the end of calamities has come. He grants the words themselves keep the same meaning either way, and that only the context decides which reason is supplied. Clarke and Wesley read it as Calvin does, the one saying there are more evils in store and they shall be carried into captivity, the other simply that God has not done with them yet. Keil and Delitzsch says this calamity Judah is preparing for itself by its obduracy and excess of wickedness.
19:
The question put into their mouths is heard two ways. Ellicott takes it as the explaining of the implied promise just given: there shall come the backward glance at the past which brings with it questionings and repentance. Calvin hears no repentance in it at all. The prophet, he says, did not soften what was severe in the threatenings but treated the people according to their perverseness, seeing they were untamable and would not bend their necks until wholly broken down; and the reason is added here so that they might not contend with God, as hypocrites are wont to do whenever he chastises them sharply, murmuring and demanding why he treats them so severely as though they were wholly innocent. Could God be constrained to render an account, they would prove him guilty of cruelty and immoderate rigour; and the description is of refractory men who will not acknowledge their fault but rise up against God with an iron front. Henry reads it the same way, that unhumbled hearts are ready to charge God with being unjust in their afflictions, though they may read their sin in their punishment; if men will inquire wherefore the Lord doeth hard things unto them, let them think of their sins. Gill simply places the speakers, the people of the Jews after they had been spoiled by the enemy and carried captive.

On the sentence itself Ellicott notes that the phrase rendered strange gods is stronger than the other gods used earlier, meaning gods of an alien race, and that the threat of serving strangers in a land that was not theirs points to the Chaldeans rather than to the Scythian invasion; with this, he says, the section that began a few verses before comes to an end. Keil and Delitzsch sets the answer down in its own balance, that as they forsook the Lord and served strange gods in their land, so shall they serve strangers in a land that is not theirs.

What the command to declare is, and to whom it is given, divides the readers again. Gill observes that the verbs are plural and so the words do not seem addressed to the prophet but to others, and takes them rather as an order to declare war against the people even in their own land. Calvin builds on the same custom: wars were usually proclaimed by heralds, enemies not marching forth at once but proclaiming war that the cause might appear just, and so God declares he had spoken in earnest by the mouth of his prophet, as though war had been proclaimed in the usual manner and armed enemies were already nigh at hand. Ellicott takes the pair of verbs as marking the beginning of a fresh section, though no definitely new topic is introduced, and says the command is given by Jehovah not to the prophet only but to his disciples. Keil and Delitzsch agrees that the exhortation is addressed to all the prophet's hearers who have the welfare of the people at heart, and adds that the word this looks forward to the chiding statement further on, that the people fears not God; the reproof of sins is introduced by an apostrophe to the hardened race. Henry gives the errand a different colour again: the prophet, having reproved them for sin and threatened the judgments of God, is here sent to them once more upon another errand which he must publish, and the purport of it is to persuade them to fear God, which would be an effectual principle of their reformation, since the want of that fear had been at the bottom of their apostasy. Wesley confines the two names, saying that by Judah and Jacob we are to understand the two tribes only.
21:
The address is read as irony, not description. Calvin says the heart in Hebrew means the mind or understanding, so the charge is that the people were destitute of it; he calls them foolish, and since many are slow and heavy yet not without common sense he adds that they are without understanding. The mention of eyes and ears seems at first a correction of that charge, but its object was ironically to enhance it and to shew them no less stupid than blocks of wood or stones: ye have ears and eyes, but ye neither see nor hear. He prefers the future tense, since their obstinacy is thereby more fully expressed, eyes they have but they will not see; and he notes that the two last lines only explain the two first in reverse order, as the prophets usually do. The this they were to hear is contained in the next verse. Ellicott calls the phrase an almost verbal reproduction from the older prophet. Wesley makes the wilfulness explicit: they are wilfully blind and obstinately deaf, and will neither see nor hear the word, will, or works of God, of which two instances follow.

The sand is handled as an argument. Clarke puts it as a question from God: what can I not do, who confine that enormous mass of waters and keep it from overflowing the earth, not by mountains and rocks but by the sand, no particle of which is in cohesion with another, so that the most tremendous waves cannot displace nor pass this simple barrier. Ellicott takes the greatness of the Lord to be shown by the majesty of his work in nature, and suggests something of the wonder of one dwelling in an inland village, to whom breaking billows were an unfamiliar sight; even the forces which seem wildest and least restrained are subject to an overruling law, and even the sand which seems so shifting keeps in the surging waters. Calvin argues it from the shape of things. It is monstrous stupidity not to fear at the presence of God when even inanimate elements obey his bidding, and the sea is the example because nothing is more terrific than a tempestuous sea; yet however furious its tossings they are under restraint. Since water, like the other elements, is spherical, and being lighter than the earth stands above it, it cannot of itself stand in one place; only some secret power of God confines it, according to what is said by Moses when the dry land was bidden to appear. Gill draws the moral from the other side, that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so where it is wanting there is nothing but ignorance and stupidity.

The contrast is then turned back on the people. Gill says they are not so obedient as the waves, nor so firm and stable as the sand set for their bound. Ellicott locates the contrast in the will: the elements are subject to God, but man's rebellious will, with its fatal gift of freedom, has power to resist, and the two adjectives are the negative and positive aspects of apostasy, joined as in the law. Keil and Delitzsch says the heart is stubborn and rebellious and bows not beneath the almighty hand of God, and rejects a derivation making the next verb mean they defy, taking it from the root meaning to turn away, so that they go off and consider not that they owe their bread to the Lord. Calvin reads the same word as a reduplicate participle with expansive force, meaning either a heart continually turning away from God or one resolutely determined to, and prefers the latter; when they revolted they were exhorted to return, and disobeyed. Clarke states the end of it plainly, that they have abandoned him and gone farther into transgression, entirely away from truth and righteousness.
24:
The charge is that a thought never occurred to them; Gill puts it flatly, that it came not into their mind. Calvin notes that the verb means in Hebrew to weigh or to consider,, and uses it to take away every pretence of ignorance: they had all the faculties belonging to men, God gave them rain, there was no year in which the earth did not bring forth its fruit, and when they ate bread the bounty of God did not occur to their minds. The blessings were felt by every part of the body, and still they did not consider that he ought to be worshipped.

Ellicott marks a turn in the argument. The former appeal, in what he calls the prophet's natural theology, was drawn from law amid what seemed the lawless elements of nature; the appeal now is from regularity of succession. On the rains he corrects the common picture: in the climate as it is now there are not two distinct rainy seasons, the whole period from autumn to spring having that character, the early rains coming in autumn and the latter closing it. The clause about the weeks he renders literally as the weeks, the ordinances, of the harvest, the seven weeks from the beginning of the barley harvest at the Passover. Clarke keeps the two seasons distinct, the early rains falling in the north about the end of September and the latter before harvest in March and April, harvest being earlier in the south. He reports a rival rendering, that a sufficiency of the appointed things of harvest is secured to us, resting on reading the word for weeks with a different sibilant so that it signifies fullness; two old versions read it so, but he prefers the present reading, since God appoints a harvest time and generally gives harvest weather. Wesley divides the rains by their office, the former to prepare the ground for sowing and the latter the corn for ripening, and draws the lesson that it is foolish as well as wicked to set oneself against the God who keeps the order of nature at his own disposal.

The withholding is then traced to its cause. Keil and Delitzsch says the people has by its sins brought about the withdrawal of these blessings, and that the second clause only repeats the first, the good being what God bestowed. Gill fills in the history, that of late years the rain had been withheld and they had neither the rains in season nor the appointed weeks, so the land was barren and famine ensued; this was to be ascribed not to any want of goodness or faithfulness in God but to their own iniquities, the mercies kept back to humble them. Ellicott says the same more guardedly, that from the prophet's point of view the rain and harvest were withheld in consequence of the people's sins. Henry states the principle, that sin stops the current of God's favour and deprives us of the blessings we used to receive, making the heavens as brass and the earth as iron. Clarke turns it into a question: when the appointed weeks of harvest do not come, should we not examine whether this be in God's judgments? Calvin has the hypocrite's objection in view: the preaching of God's paternal bounty is very well, but heat at one time burns the corn and unseasonable rains at another destroy the provisions, so nothing is certain. The answer is that their own wickedness prevents God from so regulating the year that his continued bounty could be seen. His favour does not shine out so continually but that many clouds intercept our view, and hence ungodly men think the years barren or fruitful by chance; we do not consider whence the confusion proceeds, that we obstruct his access and throw heaven and earth into confusion by our sins.
26:
Calvin will not let the charge be narrowed. Interpreters, he says, confine the words to some among the people and mistake the prophet; this is a general condemnation of the whole people whom God had chosen, as though the wicked were not to be sought among the heathen at all, iniquity so reigning among the elect people that there is in them nothing sound. On the word found he takes the sense to be convicted, their sins not secret so that they could escape by evasions, but found as thieves are found in the very act. Gill reads it the same way, that not a few only but the people in general appeared so upon inquiry, since otherwise it would not have been so hard to find a good man among them.

The fowling image is then worked out. Clarke describes the practice: the metaphor is taken from fowlers who, having fixed their nets, lie down out of sight, so that when birds come they may be ready to draw and entangle them. Ellicott notices a change of number the English hides: literally he lieth in wait, the word used elsewhere of the leopard, and then they have set the snare, the indefinite singular giving the picture of isolated guilt and the plural that of confederate evil. Wesley supplies instances, the trap Jezebel laid for Naboth and the conspiracy of more than forty men against Paul.

What the cage is divides them. Clarke has no doubt it is a decoy or trap-cage, in which fowlers put several tame birds, and when the wild ones see them they light on the cage and fall into the snare. Gill reports two Jewish expositors for a place in which fowls are fattened, and an old version that makes it a snare, but inclines to a decoy in which many birds allure others, so that it becomes very full. Ellicott keeps it simple, the large wicker basket in which the fowler kept the birds he had caught. Calvin rejects the trap-cage outright: it was a basket to keep birds in, since fowlers carry bags or cages when they go for game, and the comparison is between a cage filled with birds caught by snares and houses filled with spoils procured by frauds. He adds that strictly the houses were full not of deceit but of what deceit acquired.

The prosperity of the great is handled last. Calvin sees the prophet turning from the people at large to the higher orders, the king's counsellors, the priests, the judges, all endowed with authority, who wished to be deemed inviolable because they were rulers; he grants that they are bright and all over gold, then asks whence the splendour comes which dazzles the eyes of the simple. It availed them nothing that their aspect terrified people and their riches gained respect. Gill takes the fatness literally, that becoming rich they grew fat and their faces shone, as good living makes them. Keil and Delitzsch reads the shining the same way, of fat bodies grown glossy through the luxurious living their wealth allows, and sets aside the sense the verb bears in a cognate tongue as yielding nothing here. On the next clause Ellicott prefers they exceed in deeds of wickedness, the English being ambiguous, and observes that the prophet dwells not only on their prosperity but on their callous indifference to the poor; Wesley reads it as going beyond the heathens themselves. Calvin notes that expounders differ here, two versions omitting the words in part and one reading them as passing by the word of God. On the closing clause Ellicott prefers so that the fatherless may prosper, that being the result they do not judge with a view to, though he allows the words may mean that the wicked themselves may prosper, all they cared for; Clarke would render it a question, and shall they prosper.
29:
The refrain returns, and the readers ask why. Keil and Delitzsch calls it a refrain-like repetition of a question asked earlier, and treats the two verses that follow as an addition made after the conclusion, in which the depravity already described is briefly characterised and asserted of all ranks. Calvin says the repetition is not useless, the people having become so torpid that all reproofs were regarded with indifference; God reasons from his own office: it belongs to a judge to punish the wicked, relieve the oppressed, and check the audacity of those who allow themselves every liberty, and being God, can he suffer such impiety to prevail unpunished? On the clause about his soul he notes that God transfers to himself what does not strictly belong to him: no earthly judge is so void of feeling as to bear such indignities.

The horrible thing is weighed for force and reference. Ellicott would render the first word terrible rather than wonderful, and the verb has come to pass. Gill takes it of what may raise admiration in some and horror in others, so amazing it can hardly be conceived and so shameful it cannot be expressed. Calvin makes the same point from the pair of words, that the impiety could neither be put into words nor conceived by the mind; literally, amazement and horribleness has been done. Clarke gives another translator's rendering, strange crimes and horrible trespasses have been committed in the land, and raises the question of direction: these have been detailed already, though the phrase may refer to what follows. Wesley presses the article, that the Hebrew reads this land, aggravating the wonder that such a thing should be in such a land.

The collusion behind it is then described. Gill states what the false prophets said, that the people would have peace and not be carried into Babylon, as the true prophets had predicted. Clarke sets out the machinery: the false prophets predicted favourable things to please princes and people alike, and by their means the priests got the government into their own hands, so that both united to ruin the people, who were so infatuated that they abandoned themselves to those blind guides and would not hearken to any reformer; he quotes an old English version in which the priests flapped with joy with their hands. The middle clause is disputed. Ellicott prefers move at their hands, according to the prophets' direction, and reports two old versions making it the priests applauded with their hands, which leaves the priests following the prophets rather than leading them. Keil and Delitzsch takes the priests to rule under the prophets' guidance, and refuses the sense that they go by their side, since the verb means not to march but to trample. Calvin allows a twofold meaning, since the same verb is used of the honey taken from the lion and so may mean the priests gathered gifts into their hands; but as it also means to rule, the fitter exposition is that the priests ruled by means of the false prophets, without whom they must have been repudiated by all.

The people are not excused. Calvin anticipates their plea, that they are not learned and can only follow their teachers, and answers that the text says they love to have it so; false prophets come to try whether God's people love him from the heart, and the world is never deceived except with its own consent. Ellicott says the words imply more than acquiescence in evil and describe a settled ethical condition, the final question implying a destruction they could not avert. On what the end refers to, Calvin reports that some apply the pronoun to the prophets and priests, and takes it rather of the horrible thing itself: what will ye do when the prophets, encouraged by the priests and approved by the people, are found liars?
